prize_parts.citation: For a visionary Romanian-language prose oeuvre that builds memory, the body and dream into cumulative metaphysical architectures, rooted in a poet's attention to the sentence.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: one prize part, Mircea Cărtărescu (B006). Round 1 changed the citation scope, not the choice. The case rests on the common criteria. The voice is distinctive: dense, patterned prose in which the body, memory, dream and cosmology form one imaginative system. The formal achievement lies in architecture, meaning how Blinding (the first volume of the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid are built as large cumulative structures. The intellectual depth is the attempt to turn private perception into a cosmology. That sits in a Romanian and wider European modernist and fantastic tradition without being derivative of it. This is judged from public knowledge and the shortlist description, not from verified reading. I now narrow the citation to the prose project and name its architecture, as Palm and Sward ask. I treat the poetry as the source of the sentence-level attention, not as an independently credited body of work. That is the more defensible claim given the thin translation coverage. It also answers the chair's scope question. The fact that all six openings agree is not evidence of merit, and I do not count it. The preference stands only because the literary reasoning survives the reservations raised in round 1.
statement.case_against: The reservation remains evidential, not a change of preference. I cannot confirm how much of the density and rhythm of the Romanian survives translation, and I have no original-language expert report. Sustained quality across recursive, maximalist books is not shown by their scale. The shortlist gives only two titles, so the claim about the later work deepening rather than restating the early motifs is a judgment from general knowledge. If expert reading showed that the later volumes mostly repeat the earlier motifs, or that the translated texture is much weaker than the claim assumes, I would move to Adonis (B005). His claim on the formal and linguistic renewal of a whole poetic language is serious, and my lower placement of him reflects limits on my evidence, not a verdict on his work. I also have to guard against a risk in my own position. My Central European subject matter and my years in Prague and Vienna might make Cărtărescu's world feel familiar, and familiarity is not merit.

responses.point: Palm would keep the citation to the novelistic project so that the claim does not rest on the poetry, whose translation coverage is thinnest. She also wants it to name the formal architecture and not only the imagery. She holds that recurrence of obsessions is not a weakness in itself.
responses.response: I accept this and have rewritten my citation accordingly. It now names a prose oeuvre and its cumulative architecture, and the poetry appears only as the source of the attention to the sentence. I agree that a strong oeuvre returns to a few obsessions. The test is whether each large work enlarges the project or restates it, and neither of us can settle that without close reading of the later volumes. Where I differ from Palm is on how far her view that translation limits apply equally to every candidate lowers their weight. For Adonis the limit is real, but the claim there is about the language itself, so I would let the loss count as uncertainty and not as a reason to rank him lower on merit.

responses.point: Carlberg's citation names a prose and poetic oeuvre. She says that if the prose proves to repeat its motifs without deepening them, Adonis has the stronger claim on formal and linguistic renewal. She also says she cannot judge Arabic prosody and register from translation without expert reports.
responses.response: I take her conditional seriously, and it is close to my own. We differ on the citation. I would not credit the poetry in the citation, because I cannot confirm that its weight equals the novels' and the translation coverage is uneven. Naming it risks claiming more than we can support. I also agree with her point that the Adonis uncertainty is larger than the Cărtărescu uncertainty. That is a limit on what this committee can verify, so I would not read it as a lower literary claim. Both of us are, in effect, making a provisional judgment under limited evidence, and the committee should say so.

responses.point: Mattson calls Adonis a very close second on formal and linguistic achievement. She says her preference for Cărtărescu rests on how confidently each case can be assessed across the whole oeuvre from the evidence available. She rejects any claim that either writer is less serious.
responses.response: I agree with this framing, and it is the honest basis for my own ordering. The preference is about assessability, not a measured difference in achievement. This bears on the chair's question about Adonis. If assessability is the only difference, expert testimony on Arabic prosody and the dialogue with inherited forms could properly equalize the two, and I would then weigh them on achievement alone. I would add that the verse must stay central to any Adonis citation, with the essays named only as related critical work, as she suggests.

responses.point: Olsson says the Adonis claim, the renewal of Arabic poetic language, is very strong, but that the committee cannot verify it in the original. He therefore places Adonis just behind Cărtărescu. He also says that age and public commentary must not stand in for judgment of the poems.
responses.response: I agree on all three points, and the chair's question about whether this is a difference of evidence or of merit is the right one. On what I have, I would call it a difference of evidence. I would therefore hold my vote for Cărtărescu as provisional on the Romanian prose being tested. I would not defend it as proof that his achievement exceeds that of Adonis. I would change my vote if a Romanian-language expert report showed that the effect is mainly an artefact of scale or translation, or if an Arabic-language report confirmed Adonis's formal achievement more firmly than I can now.

responses.point: Sward says length can sustain quality or only repeat a mode. She treats her preference as provisional until readers confirm that the later volumes of the Orbitor trilogy and Solenoid develop the early ones. She wants the citation to name the cumulative architecture.
responses.response: This is the question I consider hardest, and I agree that scale alone is not sustained quality. A reading test for the later volumes would be useful: whether each volume changes the structure or the stakes, or only intensifies the same imagery. I cannot run that test from the supplied evidence and will not claim to have done so. For that reason the citation names the architecture and not the visionary style alone. I also note that her reservation and mine lead to the same condition, so it should be recorded as a shared open question and not resolved by assertion.

uncertainties: How much of the density, rhythm and syntax of the Romanian prose survives translation, including Swedish translation, cannot be judged from the supplied evidence.
Whether the later long works deepen or only restate the motifs of the Orbitor trilogy and Solenoid is unresolved. The shortlist names only two representative titles.
Whether the poetry and early fiction match the major novels is unestablished, so I leave them outside the citation scope.

The comparative weight of Adonis's poetic renewal of Arabic against large-scale prose depends on Arabic-language expert input that is not available here. It is unclear whether the gap between the two is one of evidence or of merit, and I lean toward evidence.

I have not read or independently verified any of the works. My account rests on public knowledge and the shortlist descriptions, and I make no claim about confidential proceedings or the full Academy's decision.
statement.conflict_note: Updated, and still none apparent from the supplied profile. It records no personal or professional tie between me and Cărtărescu or any other shortlisted writer. I was elected alongside Ingrid Carlberg in 2020, which is not a connection to any candidate. My Central European subject matter and long residence in Prague and Vienna are context, not evidence of preference, and I have tried to check my judgment against any pull of familiarity. This is disclosed and not adjudicated.
